Below is a quick “recipe” you can run directly in a Unix‑style shell (or adapt it to PowerShell) to pull out the very first line of *ArchivedFinalReport2024.txt*, break it up character‑by‑character, sort those characters alphabetically, and print the tidy result back onto the console.

---

### One‑liner Bash / Linux / macOS

```bash
# Grab the first line → strip newline → unfold each char → sort → rejoin
head -n 1 Archives/ArchivedFinalReport2024.txt \
| tr -d '\r\n' \                     # make sure there’s no trailing CR/LF
| fold -w1 \                         # put each character on its own line
| LC_ALL=C sort \                    # sort ASCII‑wise (fastest)
| paste -sd '' -                      # glue the sorted chars together again
```

> **Result:**  
> A single line containing *all* the original characters arranged strictly in ascending ASCII order – spaces come before digits, which come before uppercase letters, which come before lowercase letters, followed by punctuation marks, etc.

If you prefer to keep the original spacing intact but still want the words themselves sorted alphabetically, replace the middle section (`fold …`) with word‑splitting instead:

```bash
head -n 1 Archives/ArchivedFinalReport2024.txt |
tr -d '\r\n' |
awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++)print $i}' |
sort |
paste -sd ' '
```

That version outputs the individual words of the first sentence sorted alphabetically, preserving whitespace between them.


Feel free to tweak the locale (`LC_ALL=C`) if you’d rather follow Unicode code point ordering instead of pure byte values.
